title: Vibrations & waves
subtitle: From repeated motion to interference
prerequisites: Mechanics and Mathematical toolkit, including trigonometry, derivatives, integrals, ODEs, complex numbers and eigenvectors; E&M for electromagnetic sections. Each lesson links its local prerequisites.

lessons.title: A push back toward the resting point
lessons.idea: Near some stable resting positions, twice the displacement produces twice the opposing force.
body: Imagine a cart attached to a spring. Choose x=0 at its resting position and positive x to the right. Move it right: the spring pulls left. Move it left: the spring pulls right. A restoring force points back toward the resting position.

For an ideal spring, F=−kx. Here F is the signed force in newtons, x is displacement in metres and k is positive stiffness in newtons per metre. The minus sign supplies the opposite direction. A real force can often be approximated this way over a small displacement, but not over every distance.

For a smooth one-dimensional force near x=0, equilibrium means F(0)=0. The local slope F′(0) tells how much force changes per metre; the prime means a derivative with respect to position. If F′(0)<0, define k=−F′(0)>0. The first-order approximation is then F(x)≈−kx. For example, a local model slope of −50 N/m gives k=50 N/m: a small positive displacement produces a negative restoring force. A flat slope needs a different, higher-order check; not every stable force has a positive linear stiffness.

Newton’s rule gives m ẍ=−kx, or ẍ+ω₀²x=0 with ω₀=√(k/m). Two dots mean take the time derivative twice: ẍ is acceleration. The positive number ω₀ is the natural angular frequency, measured in radians per second. “Natural” means without an external repeated push or damping.

One full repeat uses 2π radians. Frequency f₀=ω₀/(2π) counts repeats per second, and period T₀=1/f₀=2π/ω₀ is the time for one repeat. These are three descriptions of the same rhythm, not three unrelated motions.
lessons.terms: F, x, ẍ: Signed force, displacement and acceleration (N, m, m/s²). The origin is the stable resting point; a dot means a time derivative. k, m: Positive stiffness and mass (N/m, kg). Here m names mass; the unit m means metre. ω₀, f₀, T₀: Natural angular frequency, frequency and period (rad/s, Hz, s). Subscript zero identifies the undamped natural rhythm. π, √: Circle constant and nonnegative square root (no unit). π≈3.14159; the square root asks what nonnegative number squares to its input. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales. F(0) is force at the origin (N); F′(0) is its position derivative there (N/m). The local linear stiffness is k=−F′(0)>0 for a negative force slope.

equationGuide.meaning: Stiffness divided by mass sets the square of the angular frequency. A stiffer spring changes motion faster; more mass changes it more slowly. Convert angular frequency to repeats per second by dividing by one full turn, 2π.

example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Use k=50 N/m and mass m=0.50 kg. At x=+0.020 m, F=−(50 N/m)(0.020 m)=−1.0 N: leftward.
ω₀=√[(50 N/m)/(0.50 kg)]=10 rad/s. The units inside the root reduce to 1/s².
f₀=10/(2π) Hz≈1.592 Hz, and T₀=2π/(10 s⁻¹)≈0.628 s. The ideal cart repeats roughly every six tenths of a second.

check.prompt: With the same mass, stiffness becomes four times as large. What happens to ω₀?
options: It becomes four times as large
explanations: The square root makes the change smaller than a factor of four.
Correct. √(4k/m)=2√(k/m).
The restoring force per displacement has changed, so the natural rhythm changes.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would a constant force pushing right produce this oscillation on its own?
apply.answer: No. A constant rightward force is not a restoring force toward a stable resting position. With no other force it gives rightward acceleration, not the sign-changing acceleration −ω₀²x. Identify the equilibrium and the local force law before using the oscillator equation.

lessons.limits: Positive mass and positive local stiffness, inertial frame, small motion if the actual force is nonlinear. Damping and external driving are absent.

glossary.definition: A position where the net force is zero.
A force pointing back toward the chosen resting position after a small displacement.

lessons.title: Read the size and timing of a repeat
lessons.idea: A sinusoid tells us how far the object can move and where it is in its repeating motion.
body: Write x(t)=A cos(ω₀t+φ). The amplitude A is the largest displacement size, not the full distance between both ends. The phase φ sets the starting point in the repeat. Use radians in the cosine; ω₀t is an angle because angular frequency is multiplied by time.

Differentiate once to get signed velocity v=−Aω₀ sin(ω₀t+φ). Differentiate again to get acceleration a=−ω₀²x. Speed is |v|, the size without its sign. The object is momentarily at rest at each end but has its largest acceleration size there.

At the resting position x=0, acceleration is zero in this ideal model, but speed is largest: Aω₀. Zero acceleration at one instant does not mean the object is stopped. Acceleration says how velocity is changing, not how large velocity already is.
lessons.terms: x, v, a: Displacement, signed velocity and acceleration (m, m/s, m/s²). All use one chosen positive direction. A: Nonnegative amplitude (m). Half the distance between the two extreme positions. ω₀, t, φ: Angular frequency, elapsed time and starting phase (rad/s, s, rad). The complete cosine/sine argument is an angle in radians; φ is not a time. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales. cm means centimetre: 1 cm=0.01 m.

equationGuide.meaning: The cosine gives displacement. Its rate of change gives velocity, and the rate of velocity gives acceleration. The three quantities peak at different times.

example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Take A=0.10 m, ω₀=10 rad/s and φ=0. At t=0, x=+0.10 m and v=0.
At t=π/(20 s⁻¹)≈0.157 s, the phase is π/2. Then x=0 and v=−1.0 m/s: the cart crosses the centre leftward.
At that crossing a=0. At the right end a=−(10 s⁻¹)²(0.10 m)=−10 m/s². Neither statement conflicts with the cart changing its motion over the full cycle.

check.prompt: Amplitude doubles while ω₀ stays fixed. What happens to the largest speed?
explanations: Correct. The largest speed is Aω₀, so it doubles with A.
The rhythm is unchanged; a longer travel distance each cycle requires greater speed.
Fixed period does not imply fixed speed when amplitude changes.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: How far apart are the two ends if A=3 cm?
apply.answer: The ends are +3 cm and −3 cm relative to equilibrium, so they are 6 cm apart. Calling 6 cm the amplitude would double-count: amplitude is the distance from the centre to one end.

lessons.limits: Undamped linear one-dimensional oscillation with fixed positive ω₀; A≥0. Phase is arbitrary and has no observable meaning when A=0.

lessons.title: Use the starting position and velocity
lessons.idea: Two starting measurements choose one motion from the family of possible oscillations.
body: Instead of guessing a phase, write x(t)=C cos(ω₀t)+D sin(ω₀t). At t=0, cosine is 1 and sine is 0, so C=x₀. The starting velocity is v₀=ω₀D, so D=v₀/ω₀. C and D can be signed; both have units of length.
The amplitude is A=√(C²+D²). These are two perpendicular coefficients in a mathematical description, not two physical travel directions. The object still moves along one line.

Energy is E=½mv²+½kx². With k=mω₀² and no damping, substitution gives the constant E=½mω₀²A². At an end all this energy is spring energy; at the centre it is kinetic energy. The energy equation checks the starting-data calculation.
lessons.equation: C=x₀;  D=v₀/ω₀;  x=C cos(ω₀t)+D sin(ω₀t);  A=√(C²+D²);  E=½mω₀²A²

C is not the coulomb unit in this equation; A is a length, not amperes. ω₀, t: Natural angular frequency and time (rad/s, s). Positive fixed ω₀; the trig arguments are radians. m, k, E: Mass, stiffness and total mechanical energy (kg, N/m, J). k=mω₀²; ½ means one half. E is constant only in the undamped, undriven model. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). steps: Use m=0.50 kg, ω₀=10 rad/s, x₀=0.060 m and v₀=+0.80 m/s. Then C=0.060 m and D=0.080 m.
A=√[(0.060 m)²+(0.080 m)²]=0.100 m. The positive starting velocity means the cart initially moves right.

check.prompt: The same x₀ is kept, but v₀ changes sign. What happens to amplitude?
explanations: Amplitude is a nonnegative size, not a direction.
Correct. D changes sign but D² does not, so A stays the same. The timing changes.
The stored spring energy and kinetic energy are not removed by reversing velocity.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If the starting position is zero but velocity is nonzero, is the amplitude zero?
apply.answer: No. C=0, but D=v₀/ω₀ is nonzero. Amplitude is |v₀|/ω₀. The object starts at the centre with kinetic energy, then moves toward an end where that energy becomes spring energy.

lessons.limits: One-dimensional undamped linear oscillator, mass>0 and ω₀>0. This does not determine a unique phase for the zero-amplitude state.

practice.prompt: Use m=2.0 kg, ω₀=5.0 rad/s, x₀=0.030 m and v₀=−0.20 m/s.
practice.reasoning: Explain why reversing the velocity changes the timing but not the total energy. Entry tolerances permit rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty. Enter a decimal or scientific-notation number, not a fraction or expression.

lessons.title: Why a small pendulum nearly repeats one rhythm
lessons.idea: For a small swing, gravity supplies an almost linear push back toward the bottom.
body: Consider a small mass on a light inextensible string of length ℓ, with a fixed pivot. Measure angle θ from the downward resting direction. Positive θ is a chosen direction of rotation. The tangential gravitational force is −mg sinθ; it points back toward the bottom for small positive or negative θ.

Tangential acceleration is ℓθ̈, so the mass cancels from mℓθ̈=−mg sinθ. The exact ideal-pendulum equation is θ̈+(g/ℓ)sinθ=0. Here θ̈ is angular acceleration. Radian angle is dimensionless in SI dimensional algebra, although we keep rad to identify angular quantities.

For a small angle in radians, sinθ≈θ. That approximation turns the equation into an oscillator with ω₀=√(g/ℓ), and period T₀=2π√(ℓ/g). The approximation concerns the size of the angle, not the size of the mass. Larger swings need the nonlinear sine equation; the small-angle period is then not exact.
lessons.terms: θ, θ̈: Angular displacement and angular acceleration (rad, rad/s²). Angle is measured from vertically downward. The dots are time derivatives. ℓ, g: String length and gravity magnitude (m, m/s²). ℓ is the pivot-to-bob length; use constant g≈9.81 m/s² here. ω₀, T₀: Approximate angular frequency and period (rad/s, s). These formulas use small-angle linearization, not arbitrary swing size. ≈, π: Approximately equal and circle constant (no unit). π≈3.14159. The approximation sinθ≈θ requires radians, not degrees. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales.

equationGuide.meaning: Gravity divided by pendulum length sets the square of the small-swing angular frequency. A longer pendulum takes more time per swing; changing the bob’s mass does not change this ideal small-swing period.

At θ=0.10 rad, sinθ≈0.09983. Replacing it by 0.10 changes the restoring-angle factor by about 0.17 percent.

check.prompt: Length is reduced to one quarter, keeping the same small angle and g. What happens to the period?
options: It becomes four times as long
explanations: Period scales with the square root of length, not its inverse.
The length appears directly in the period formula.
Correct. √(ℓ/4)=√ℓ/2, so the approximate period halves.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can the 2.006 s result be assumed exact for a 90-degree release?
apply.answer: No. Ninety degrees is π/2 radians, not a small angle: sin(π/2)=1 while π/2≈1.571. The linear restoring approximation is poor there. Keep the full sine equation or another justified nonlinear method; do not use the small-angle formula as an exact prediction.

lessons.limits: Point bob, massless fixed-length string, fixed pivot, uniform gravity, no drag; small angular amplitude for the approximate period. Not a compound or driven pendulum.

glossary.definition: Replacing a smooth relation by a simpler straight-line approximation near one chosen point.

lessons.title: Add a force that resists motion
lessons.idea: Linear drag makes each repeat smaller while preserving a simple analytic model.
body: Add a drag force −bv to the spring force, where b is positive and v=ẋ. Drag opposes velocity, not displacement. The force balance is m ẍ+b ẋ+kx=0. There is no external drive.

Define β=b/(2m), in inverse seconds, and ω₀=√(k/m). If β<ω₀, the solution is x=A e^(−βt) cos(ω_dt+φ), where ω_d=√(ω₀²−β²). The constant e≈2.718 is the natural exponential base. The decaying factor multiplies the sinusoid’s size; the oscillation is a little slower than the undamped one.

The envelope A e^(−βt) is a bound on the displacement size, not the instantaneous displacement itself. If φ=0, differentiating at t=0 gives v₀=−βA, not zero. Starting at an envelope peak is not automatically starting at rest.
lessons.equation: m ẍ+b ẋ+kx=0;  β=b/(2m);  ω_d=√(ω₀²−β²);  x=A e^(−βt)cos(ω_dt+φ)
lessons.terms: m, b, k: Mass, linear drag coefficient and stiffness (kg, kg/s, N/m). All are positive constants; b times velocity has units of force. x, ẋ, ẍ: Displacement, velocity and acceleration (m, m/s, m/s²). Dots mean time derivatives. β, ω₀, ω_d: Decay rate, natural and damped angular frequencies (s⁻¹, rad/s, rad/s). The underdamped formula requires β<ω₀. A, t, φ, e: Envelope coefficient, time, phase and exponential base (m, s, rad, no unit). A≥0; e≈2.718. The exponent −βt has no unit. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales.

equationGuide.meaning: The restoring force pulls toward equilibrium and drag resists motion. In the underdamped case, the motion repeats inside an exponentially shrinking envelope.

example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Let m=1.0 kg, b=0.40 kg/s and k=4.0 N/m. Then β=0.20 s⁻¹ and ω₀=2.0 rad/s.
ω_d=√[(2.0 s⁻¹)²−(0.20 s⁻¹)²]≈1.990 rad/s. This is less than the undamped value.
For A=0.10 m, the envelope at t=5.0 s is (0.10 m)e⁻¹≈0.0368 m. With φ=0, the initial velocity is −0.020 m/s; the model does not start at rest.

visual.title: Watch the shrinking envelope
visual.caption: Separate phase-zero model x=A exp(−βt) cos(ω_dt), with ω_d=√(ω₀²−β²). The curve traces displacement versus time, not a path through space. cm=0.01 m. Dashed curves bound the displacement; initial velocity is −βA, not generally zero. Controls keep 0≤β<ω₀. This ideal linear model includes the undamped β=0 limit; no real-device safety prediction.

check.prompt: Keep mass fixed and double b. What happens to β?
explanations: Correct. β=b/(2m), so doubling b doubles the decay rate.
Greater drag does not slow the decay in this underdamped-envelope comparison.
The drag coefficient directly enters β.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Is the damped period always exactly 2π/ω₀?
apply.answer: No. While the system remains underdamped, its repeat period is 2π/ω_d, with ω_d=√(ω₀²−β²). Only for zero damping does ω_d equal ω₀ exactly; weak damping may make the difference small.

lessons.limits: Linear spring and viscous drag, constants m,k,b>0, underdamped β<ω₀; no nonlinear friction or external forcing.

lessons.title: Decide whether the model can oscillate
lessons.idea: A drag threshold separates repeating motion from sums of nonoscillatory decays.
body: Try a time dependence e^(rt), where r is a rate in inverse seconds. Substitution into the force equation gives r²+2βr+ω₀²=0. Its roots are r=−β±√(β²−ω₀²). The quantity under the square root decides the kind of response.

If β<ω₀, the roots have imaginary parts and the real motion can oscillate while shrinking. If β=ω₀, the repeated root gives x=(C+Dt)e^(−ω₀t): critical damping. Here C is a length and D is a length per second. If β>ω₀, two distinct negative real roots give x=C e^(r₁t)+D e^(r₂t), where both C and D are lengths.

Critical and overdamped responses do not have a repeating sinusoid, but that does not guarantee that position always decreases. The starting position and velocity set the coefficients. A motion can first move farther from equilibrium and then return without repeatedly oscillating. “Fastest” claims require a stated initial condition and comparison measure.
lessons.equation: r=−β±√(β²−ω₀²);  β<ω₀: underdamped;  β=ω₀: critical;  β>ω₀: overdamped
lessons.terms: r, r₁, r₂: Characteristic time rates (s⁻¹). The exponential e^(rt) uses a dimensionless product rt. β, ω₀: Drag rate and undamped angular frequency (s⁻¹, rad/s). Radians are dimensionless in this comparison. x, t, C, D: Displacement, time and solution coefficients (m, s; coefficients as stated). D has units m/s in the critical form C+Dt, but m in the two-exponential overdamped form. ±: Two choices of sign (no unit). One root uses plus and the other uses minus. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). steps: Keep m=1.0 kg and k=4.0 N/m, so ω₀=2.0 rad/s. Critical drag is b=2mω₀=4.0 kg/s.
For b=5.0 kg/s, β=2.5 s⁻¹ and roots are −2.5±1.5 s⁻¹: −1.0 s⁻¹ and −4.0 s⁻¹. Both decay without a sinusoidal factor.

check.prompt: For m=1 kg, k=4 N/m and b=6 kg/s, which regime applies?
explanations: β=3 s⁻¹ exceeds ω₀=2 s⁻¹.
Correct. β>ω₀, so the characteristic roots are distinct negative real rates.
Critical damping would require b=4 kg/s here.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why is “no oscillation” not the same as “never crosses equilibrium”?
apply.answer: A sum of two decaying terms can have opposite signs. Depending on its starting state, that sum can cross zero once before approaching equilibrium. What is absent in the overdamped model is a repeating sinusoidal sequence, not every possible crossing.

lessons.limits: Positive mass, stiffness and drag; constant coefficients and no drive. Regime comparisons do not apply unchanged to nonlinear or time-varying damping.

lessons.title: Track where the lost oscillator energy goes
lessons.idea: Drag transfers mechanical energy away, but displacement and energy do not decay at the same rate.
body: For the spring oscillator, mechanical energy is E=½mv²+½kx². Differentiate and use the force equation: dE/dt=−bv². Since b>0 and v²≥0, mechanical energy cannot grow without a drive in this model. The lost energy transfers to the surroundings; it is not destroyed.

The underdamped displacement envelope falls as e^(−βt). Energy is quadratic in displacement and velocity. When damping is weak, a cycle-averaged energy envelope therefore falls approximately as e^(−2βt). The instantaneous energy can vary within that smooth envelope; do not replace the exact power law by an exact cycle-average identity.

The amplitude e-folding time is 1/β; the weak-damping energy e-folding time is 1/(2β). An e-fold means a factor 1/e. For weak damping, quality factor Q≈ω₀/(2β) describes how many radians of oscillation fit into substantial energy loss. More precisely, Q≈2π times stored energy divided by energy lost in one cycle when that loss is small.
lessons.terms: E, E₀, ⟨E⟩: Mechanical energy, reference energy and cycle-average energy (J). Angle brackets mean an average over a repeat, not an instantaneous value. b, v, dE/dt: Drag coefficient, signed velocity and energy-change rate (kg/s, m/s, W). The square v² makes the mechanical-energy rate nonpositive. A_env, A₀: Current and reference amplitude envelopes (m). These are bounds on oscillating displacement. β, ω₀, t, Q: Decay rate, natural angular frequency, time and quality factor (s⁻¹, rad/s, s, no unit). The envelope/Q interpretation assumes β much smaller than ω₀; β is positive. steps: Use m=1.0 kg, ω₀=10 rad/s and b=0.20 kg/s, so β=0.10 s⁻¹ and Q≈50. Damping is weak compared with the oscillation rate.
At v=0.30 m/s, dE/dt=−(0.20 kg/s)(0.30 m/s)²=−0.018 W. This exact instantaneous rate is negative.
After 5.0 s, the amplitude envelope is e⁻⁰·⁵≈0.607 of its reference size; the approximate cycle-average energy is e⁻¹≈0.368 of its reference value. Those are different fractions.

visual.title: Keep the pieces separate
visual.caption: Envelope and Q estimates are cycle-averaged, weak-damping statements; the exact instantaneous energy balance is dE/dt=−bv².

check.prompt: In weak damping, what fraction of energy remains when the amplitude envelope has halved?
explanations: Energy scales with amplitude squared in this approximation.
A passive drag-only oscillator does not gain mechanical energy.
Correct. The approximate energy envelope scales as the square, so (1/2)²=1/4.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does the negative dE/dt mean total energy has vanished?
apply.answer: No. This E counts only mechanical energy of the chosen oscillator. The drag interaction transfers energy into other degrees of freedom, often thermal motion in the surroundings. Enlarging the system boundary restores the full energy accounting.

lessons.limits: Exact power balance for linear viscous drag and spring. Exponential cycle-energy envelope and cycle-loss definition of Q require weak damping; no claims about structural or acoustic safety.

practice.prompt: A weakly damped oscillator has m=2.0 kg, b=0.40 kg/s and ω₀=8.0 rad/s.
practice.reasoning: Explain why the negative velocity does not reverse the sign of energy loss. Entry tolerances permit rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty. Enter a decimal or scientific-notation number, not a fraction or expression.

lessons.title: Separate the repeated response from the start-up
lessons.idea: A regular push can produce a regular motion after the starting disturbance fades.
body: Let an external force be F₀ cos(ωt), where F₀ is a nonnegative peak force and ω is the chosen drive angular frequency. The equation is m ẍ+b ẋ+kx=F₀ cos(ωt). The drive frequency is chosen by the source; it need not equal the natural frequency √(k/m).

With positive damping, the initial-condition part eventually decays. The remaining steady response has the drive frequency: x=A cos(ωt−δ). Here A is displacement amplitude and δ is its phase lag behind the force. “Steady” does not mean motionless; it means the repeating response no longer changes from cycle to cycle.

The amplitude is A=F₀/√[(k−mω²)²+(bω)²]. Both k−mω² and bω have units N/m, so the denominator is force per displacement. Dividing force by it gives a length. This formula predicts the steady response, not the position immediately after the drive is switched on.
lessons.terms: m, b, k: Mass, drag coefficient and stiffness (kg, kg/s, N/m). All positive and fixed; the spring and damping laws are linear. F₀, ω, t: Peak drive force, drive angular frequency and time (N, rad/s, s). F₀≥0 and ω>0; the force is sinusoidal. x, ẋ, ẍ: Displacement, velocity and acceleration (m, m/s, m/s²). Measured from the chosen equilibrium. A, δ: Steady displacement amplitude and phase lag (m, rad). A≥0; lag enters as minus δ in x=A cos(ωt−δ). Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales.

equationGuide.meaning: The drive must overcome the spring/inertia balance and damping. Their combined size determines how much displacement a given peak force produces after transients die away.

example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Take m=1.0 kg, k=4.0 N/m, b=0.40 kg/s and F₀=0.080 N. Drive at ω=2.0 rad/s, the natural frequency.
Then k−mω²=0 and bω=0.80 N/m. The amplitude is A=(0.080 N)/(0.80 N/m)=0.100 m.
Driving instead at ω=1.0 rad/s gives a denominator √[(3.0 N/m)²+(0.40 N/m)²]≈3.027 N/m and A≈0.0264 m. Same force, different response size.

visual.caption: A linear steady-state response with positive damping; a large ideal amplitude may exceed the small-motion regime of a real device.

check.prompt: In this linear model, F₀ doubles with all other parameters fixed. What happens to steady amplitude?
explanations: The denominator is unchanged, so a stronger force cannot halve A here.
Drive size appears directly in the numerator.
Correct. A is proportional to F₀ when the model parameters and frequency are fixed.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can this steady formula describe a truly undamped oscillator driven exactly at its natural frequency?
apply.answer: No. With b=0 and ω=ω₀ the denominator vanishes, signalling that a bounded steady sinusoid is not the right solution. The resonant response grows with elapsed driving time in the ideal model. It does not become infinitely large at the instant the drive starts.

lessons.limits: Constant positive mass, stiffness and damping; fixed sinusoidal drive, late-time steady response and linear displacement range. Transients and nonlinear saturation are separate.

lessons.title: Track when the response happens
lessons.idea: Two motions can share a frequency while reaching their peaks at different times.
body: Use force F=F₀ cos(ωt) and displacement x=A cos(ωt−δ). A positive δ means the displacement peak comes later than the force peak. One full cycle is 2π radians; δ/ω is the corresponding delay within this sinusoidal description.

The correct quadrant matters. Define Δ=k−mω² and B=bω, both in N/m. The lag δ is the angle of the point (Δ,B) in the complex plane: δ=atan2(B,Δ). This two-input angle function uses both signs, unlike a bare arctangent of B/Δ. With b>0 and ω>0, B is positive, so 0<δ<π.

Below the natural frequency, Δ>0 and the lag is less than a quarter cycle. At ω₀=√(k/m), Δ=0 and δ=π/2. Above it, Δ<0 and the lag exceeds π/2, approaching π for very large ω. Velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle, so at ω₀ the velocity—not displacement—is in phase with the force.
lessons.terms: Δ, B: Spring/inertia difference and damping contribution (N/m). B is a local name here, not magnetic field. Δ here names a difference, not a derivative. δ, atan2: Displacement phase lag and quadrant-aware angle function (rad). atan2(B,Δ) returns the angle of coordinates (Δ,B); use the correct quadrant. m, k, b, ω: Mass, stiffness, drag and driving angular frequency (kg, N/m, kg/s, rad/s). m,k,b,ω are positive. x, A, t: Displacement, amplitude and time (m, m, s). The drive phase is ωt. Velocity is the derivative of x. visual.caption: Phase convention is fixed by F₀cos(ωt) and x=Acos(ωt−δ). Different written conventions must be translated, not mixed.

check.prompt: At ω=ω₀ with positive damping, which statement is correct?
options: Velocity and force are in phase
explanations: Displacement lags the force by π/2 in this convention.
Correct. Velocity leads displacement by π/2, cancelling the displacement’s lag behind the force.
The steady motion continues; zero velocity occurs only at its turning points.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why is “the phase is 180 degrees” alone incomplete?
apply.answer: It must say which two quantities are being compared and under which written convention. Here δ compares displacement with the sinusoidal force, with x=A cos(ωt−δ). A phase for velocity or for an e^(−iωt) convention must be translated before comparing it with this δ.

lessons.limits: Positive linear damping, positive drive frequency, nonzero drive amplitude and late-time steady response. At zero amplitude a measured displacement phase is undefined.

lessons.title: Average power measures useful energy transfer
lessons.idea: A force transfers energy through motion only when its timing matches the velocity.
body: Instantaneous power delivered by the drive is Fv, not Fx. Multiply the sinusoidal force and velocity, then average over a full cycle. Terms that are positive and negative equally often cancel; the remaining mean is ⟨P_in⟩=½F₀Aω sinδ. The amplitudes here are peaks: the largest absolute values over a cycle. RMS, mentioned below, means root mean square: square the instantaneous values, average over the cycle, then take the nonnegative square root.

The damper dissipates power bv². Since the average of sine squared is one half, its mean loss is ⟨P_loss⟩=½bω²A². These means are equal in steady state because the oscillator’s stored energy returns to the same value after each cycle.

At fixed force amplitude F₀, the largest absorbed mean power occurs at ω₀=√(k/m) in this ideal model. The displacement-amplitude peak can be at a different frequency because power also depends on velocity. A peak in one measured quantity is not automatically a peak in every quantity.
lessons.terms: ⟨P_in⟩, ⟨P_loss⟩: Cycle-average input and dissipated power (W). Angle brackets mean average over one complete drive cycle. F₀, A, ω, δ: Peak force, displacement amplitude, drive angular frequency and displacement lag (N, m, rad/s, rad). These are peak amplitudes, not RMS values. Aω is peak speed. b: Linear damping coefficient (kg/s). Positive. The product bω²A² has units joules per second. steps: Use F₀=0.080 N, A=0.100 m, ω=2.0 rad/s, b=0.40 kg/s and δ=π/2.

check.prompt: F₀ doubles at the same frequency and fixed linear parameters. How does mean dissipated power change?
options: It becomes four times as large
explanations: Correct. A doubles, and mean loss is proportional to A², so it becomes four times as large.
Power depends on the product of force and velocity; both response amplitude and force change here.
More drive force changes the steady energy transfer.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can the mean power be zero even when a nonzero sinusoidal force acts?
apply.answer: Yes in an ideal lossless off-resonant steady response, where force and velocity are a quarter cycle apart. Positive and negative instantaneous transfers cancel over a cycle. That is a different limit from resonant undamped growth and from the positive-damping steady model used for the numerical example.

lessons.limits: Linear viscous damping, fixed positive b,m,k, sinusoidal steady state. Peak conventions explicit; no real-machine power or safety rating.

lessons.title: Name which resonance peak you mean
lessons.idea: A response curve needs a measured quantity and a width definition before its peak is meaningful.
body: For a fixed peak force, the displacement amplitude is largest at ω_r=√(ω₀²−2β²), provided β<ω₀/√2. Here β=b/(2m). If damping is stronger, there is no positive-frequency displacement peak; the largest amplitude over nonnegative frequency is the static limit.

The absorbed-power peak is instead at ω₀. Define its half-power width Δω as the upper frequency minus the lower frequency where mean absorbed power is half its peak value. Width is not the same as amplitude, and half power is not half displacement.

For a narrow, weak-damping resonance, the two half-power frequencies lie approximately at ω₀−β and ω₀+β. Thus Δω≈2β and Q≈ω₀/Δω. These near-peak approximations require β≪ω₀. Even a sharp ideal resonance takes time to build after switching on the drive.
lessons.equation: ω_r=√(ω₀²−2β²) if β<ω₀/√2;  Δω≈2β;  Q≈ω₀/Δω (weak damping)
lessons.terms: ω_r, ω₀: Displacement-peak and natural angular frequencies (rad/s). The power peak, not the displacement peak, is at ω₀ for this force-driven linear model. β, Δω: Decay rate and full half-power width (s⁻¹, rad/s). Δω is upper minus lower half-power frequency; radian is dimensionless in the algebra. Q: Approximate quality factor (no unit). The width and cycle-loss interpretations agree in weak damping. ≪: Much smaller than (no unit). This flags an approximation, not equality. example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Let ω₀=10 rad/s and β=0.20 s⁻¹. The displacement peak is √(100−0.08) rad/s≈9.996 rad/s.
The weak-damping power half-height frequencies are about 9.8 and 10.2 rad/s, giving Δω≈0.40 rad/s.
Q≈10/0.40=25. The small peak shift does not mean the two peak definitions are identical; it means this damping is weak.

check.prompt: For fixed ω₀ in the weak-damping regime, β is halved. What happens to the approximate power width?
explanations: The width is proportional to β, not inversely proportional.
Changing the damping changes the width.
Correct. Δω≈2β, so halving β halves the approximate width and doubles Q.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why should a measured peak be labelled “displacement” or “power”?
apply.answer: The formulas maximize different functions of frequency. Power depends on velocity and its timing relative to the drive, while displacement amplitude has a shifted maximum. Naming the observable prevents treating two close but distinct resonances as exactly the same.

lessons.limits: Constant-force-amplitude linear oscillator. Positive-frequency displacement peak requires β<ω₀/√2. Half-power locations and Q interpretation shown here are weak-damping approximations.

lessons.title: The middle spring links two motions
lessons.idea: Each cart’s force depends on its own position and on the other cart’s position.
body: Place two equal carts in a line. Each cart is attached to its outer wall by a spring of stiffness k, and the carts are joined by a spring of stiffness κ. Let x₁ and x₂ be rightward displacements from the shared equilibrium configuration, not the absolute distances from a wall.

The middle spring’s change of length is x₂−x₁. It pulls cart 1 right with force κ(x₂−x₁), and cart 2 left with the opposite force. Adding each wall spring gives m ẍ₁=−(k+κ)x₁+κx₂ and m ẍ₂=κx₁−(k+κ)x₂.

The cross terms describe coupling: motion of one cart affects the acceleration of the other. They have positive signs on the right-hand side under this displacement convention. The middle-spring forces cancel in the two-cart total force, but the wall forces do not.
lessons.terms: x₁, x₂, ẍ₁, ẍ₂: Cart displacements and accelerations (m, m/s²). Both positive directions are right. Subscripts label carts. m: Mass of each cart (kg). Equal positive masses; not the combined mass. k, κ: Each wall stiffness and middle stiffness (N/m). Kappa κ is a second spring stiffness; both are positive here. example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Use m=1.0 kg, k=9.0 N/m and κ=8.0 N/m. Put x₁=+0.020 m and x₂=0.
The first net force is −(17 N/m)(0.020 m)=−0.340 N. The second is +(8 N/m)(0.020 m)=+0.160 N.
Accelerations are −0.340 m/s² and +0.160 m/s². Total force is −0.180 N, exactly the net wall force −k(x₁+x₂); the internal spring does not push the whole pair by itself.

check.prompt: If both carts are displaced equally rightward, what is the middle spring’s change of length?
explanations: The difference x₂−x₁ is zero when the displacements are equal.
Correct. Equal translation of both carts leaves the middle spring length unchanged.
A single displacement is not the relative extension of the middle spring.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can one solve cart 1 as an isolated spring with stiffness k+κ while cart 2 is free to move?
apply.answer: Not generally. The term κx₂ is then changing, so cart 1 is not an independent oscillator with a fixed external endpoint. Holding cart 2 fixed is a different physical constraint. Use both coupled equations unless a valid special motion or constraint simplifies them.

lessons.limits: Equal positive masses and wall stiffnesses, positive coupling stiffness, small linear displacements, frictionless motion and fixed walls. No damping or driving.

lessons.title: Find two motions that keep their shape
lessons.idea: In a normal mode, the relative motion of the carts stays fixed while their common time factor oscillates.
body: First try equal displacements: x₁=x₂. The middle spring does not stretch. Each cart feels only its wall restoring force, so this symmetric mode has ω_s=√(k/m). Both carts move together.

Next try opposite displacements: x₁=−x₂. The middle spring changes length twice as much as either cart moves. Each cart behaves as if the restoring stiffness were k+2κ, giving the antisymmetric frequency ω_a=√[(k+2κ)/m]. “Antisymmetric” here simply means equal size with opposite sign.

These two displacement patterns are eigenvectors of the stiffness matrix: (1,1) and (1,−1). Their entries describe a ratio, not a position measured in metres until multiplied by a length coefficient. A normal mode is a coordinated motion pattern, not an extra physical object.

Subscripts identify patterns, not two different mass values. m, k, κ: Each mass, wall stiffness and middle stiffness (kg, N/m, N/m). All positive; the symmetric wall arrangement matters. x₁, x₂, ∝: Displacements and proportional-to sign (m; no unit for ∝). The pattern vectors (1,1) and (1,−1) contain dimensionless ratios. steps: Use m=1.0 kg, k=9.0 N/m and κ=8.0 N/m. Then ω_s=3.0 rad/s and ω_a=5.0 rad/s.

check.prompt: Increase κ but keep k and m fixed. Which frequency changes?
explanations: The symmetric mode does not stretch the middle spring.
The opposite-motion mode stretches it, so its restoring force changes.
Correct. ω_s depends only on k/m; ω_a depends on k+2κ.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does a normal-mode pattern require the carts to remain motionless relative to the room?
apply.answer: No. Their displacements generally change with time. What remains fixed is their displacement ratio: equal for the symmetric mode or opposite for the antisymmetric mode. The whole pattern is multiplied by a sinusoidal time factor.

lessons.limits: Undamped symmetric two-mass system with equal wall springs. Pattern labels describe this geometry; they do not replace a general normal-mode calculation.

lessons.title: Build a motion from both patterns
lessons.idea: One cart released on its own generally excites both normal modes.
body: Let cart 1 start at displacement a and cart 2 at zero, with both initially at rest. Add equal amounts of the two mode patterns: x₁=(a/2)[cos(ω_st)+cos(ω_at)] and x₂=(a/2)[cos(ω_st)−cos(ω_at)]. At t=0 these give x₁=a and x₂=0, and both derivatives vanish.

Define the mean angular frequency ω̄=(ω_a+ω_s)/2 and the half-difference Δω=(ω_a−ω_s)/2. Trig identities give x₁=a cos(ω̄t)cos(Δωt) and x₂=a sin(ω̄t)sin(Δωt). A bar means mean here; Δω is a half-difference in this lesson, not the full resonance width used earlier.

When the frequencies are close, the fast factors oscillate inside slowly changing envelopes. Mechanical energy moves between the carts and springs, while total energy stays constant. Assigning a separate “energy of cart 1” requires a convention for sharing the middle-spring energy. Do not infer perfect energy transfer just because one displacement envelope reaches zero.

steps: Use m=1.0 kg, k=361 N/m, κ=40 N/m and a=0.010 m. The mode frequencies are 19 and 21 rad/s, so ω̄=20 rad/s and Δω=1 rad/s.
At t=0, x₁=0.010 m, x₂=0 and both speeds are zero. Total energy is ½(k+κ)a²=0.02005 J.

explanations: Correct. Adding the two a/2 patterns gives (a,0).
That would give initial cart-1 displacement 2a.
A pure symmetric mode would initially displace both carts equally.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If cart 1 is momentarily at x₁=0, has it necessarily lost all kinetic energy?
apply.answer: No. Kinetic energy depends on velocity, not position. The worked case has x₁=0 but v₁≠0. To discuss energy exchange, compute velocities and include the spring energies; the displacement picture alone is insufficient.

lessons.limits: Linear undamped symmetric system. Slow-envelope interpretation requires nearby mode frequencies; the original two-cosine sum itself does not require weak coupling.

practice.prompt: Two carts each have mass 2.0 kg, wall stiffness k=8.0 N/m and middle stiffness κ=5.0 N/m. Release cart 1 from a=0.020 m and cart 2 from zero, both at rest.

lessons.title: Find a motion that keeps its shape
lessons.idea: A normal mode is a pattern whose parts keep the same size ratio while they swing.
body: A normal mode is a pattern whose parts keep the same size ratio while they swing.

Collect the displacements in a column x. The mass matrix M turns acceleration into force. The stiffness matrix K turns displacement into the opposite of restoring force. With no damping or drive, M ẍ + K x = 0. A double dot means two time derivatives.

Try x = a cos(ωt). The column a gives the signed displacement amplitudes. Two derivatives give ẍ = −ω²x. Substitution leaves K a = ω² M a. A nonzero a exists only when det(K − ω²M) = 0: the determinant tests whether this matrix can squash a nonzero column to zero.

For a stable supported system with positive masses and positive stiffness energy, squared frequencies are positive. A zero result instead can describe a free motion with no restoring force; a negative result does not describe a stable oscillation.
lessons.equation: K a = ω² M a; det(K − ω²M) = 0
lessons.terms: K: stiffness matrix (N/m). Its entries connect each displacement to each restoring force. M: mass matrix (kg). For two separate equal masses it is m₀ times the identity matrix I; m₀ is each mass in kg. I leaves a column unchanged. a: mode amplitude column (m). Its entries may have opposite signs. Multiplying all entries by one constant preserves the mode shape. ω: natural angular frequency (rad/s). ω² has numerical units s⁻²; cos uses the dimensionless phase ωt. x, t: displacement column and time (m; s). The double dot is acceleration in m/s²; det means determinant. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Choose M = (2 kg) I and K = [[10, −2], [−2, 10]] N/m. These are a stated ideal two-coordinate model.
For a = (0.01, 0.01) m, K a = (0.08, 0.08) N. Dividing each component by the matching M a component gives ω² = 4 s⁻², so ω = 2 rad/s.
For a = (0.01, −0.01) m, K a = (0.12, −0.12) N. Now ω² = 6 s⁻², so ω ≈ 2.449 rad/s. The characteristic equation is (10 − 2ω²)² − 4 = 0 when numbers are expressed in these SI units.

explanations: More mass slows the response; it does not speed it up.
Correct: ω² is halved, so ω is divided by √2.
The stiffness is unchanged, but the mass in the eigenproblem changed.

apply.text: Is (−0.01, −0.01) m a new mode?
apply.answer: No. It is the same in-phase shape with the opposite overall sign.

lessons.title: Build the starting motion from modes
lessons.idea: A complicated starting shape can be assembled from simpler mode shapes.
body: A complicated starting shape can be assembled from simpler mode shapes.

For equal masses, choose dimensionless mode columns e₁ and e₂ of length one and at right angles. These are orthonormal: each dot product with itself is 1 and their mutual dot product is 0. A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them.

The coordinate qⱼ tells how much of mode j is present. Project the initial displacement and velocity onto eⱼ. Each qⱼ then follows its own undamped oscillator. Add eⱼ qⱼ to recover the physical displacement; the mode coordinates are not extra masses.
lessons.equation: qⱼ(0) = eⱼ·x(0); q̇ⱼ(0) = eⱼ·u(0); qⱼ(t) = qⱼ(0) cos(ωⱼt) + [q̇ⱼ(0)/ωⱼ] sin(ωⱼt); x(t) = Σⱼ eⱼ qⱼ(t)
lessons.terms: eⱼ: unit mode column (dimensionless). j labels a mode; Σ means add the listed modes. qⱼ, x: mode coordinate and displacement column (m). q is a coefficient multiplying a mode shape. u, q̇ⱼ: physical velocity and mode-coordinate velocity (m/s). A single dot means one time derivative. ωⱼ, t: positive natural angular frequency and time (rad/s; s). The formula divides by ωⱼ, so it excludes a zero-frequency mode. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

steps: Both q₁(0) and q₂(0) are 0.02/√2 m ≈ 0.014142 m; both starting mode velocities vanish.
With ω₁ = 2 rad/s and ω₂ = √6 rad/s, x₁(t) = (0.01 m)[cos((2 rad/s)t) + cos((√6 rad/s)t)] and x₂(t) is the same expression with a minus between the cosines. At t = 0 this gives (0.02,0) m.

The opposite-sign mode needs a difference between the initial displacements.
The nonzero in-phase displacement gives a nonzero e₁ projection.

apply.title: Change the situation
apply.text: What if the starting displacement is zero but the velocity is not?
apply.answer: Project the velocity too. The sine coefficient q̇ⱼ(0)/ωⱼ then creates motion even when the cosine coefficient is zero.

lessons.limits: Equal masses and a complete orthonormal mode basis; undamped linear motion with positive frequencies. Unequal masses require mass-weighted projection, not this ordinary dot-product recipe.

lessons.title: A force pattern can miss a mode
lessons.idea: A push excites a mode only through the part of the push that matches that mode.
body: A push excites a mode only through the part of the push that matches that mode.
Use the same unit mode columns as before. Dot the force column F with a mode column eⱼ to get its modal force Fⱼ. Equal pushes on both masses have no component along an opposite-sign mode.

If each equal mass has the same independent drag coefficient b, the same modes stay separate. Their equations contain inertia, drag and restoring force. An initially resting mode with zero modal force stays at rest. A mode already moving may still have a decaying free response.

A nonzero sinusoidal modal drive has the damped response taught earlier. Being near a natural frequency matters only if the drive projects onto that mode. With no damping, a resonant drive need not settle to a bounded steady motion.

lessons.terms: F, Fⱼ: physical force column and projected modal force (N). The dot product adds signed matching components. eⱼ: unit mode column (dimensionless). Here e₁=(1,1)/√2 and e₂=(1,−1)/√2. m₀, b: each mass and its drag coefficient (kg; kg/s). The same b acts independently on both masses. qⱼ, ωⱼ, t: mode displacement, natural angular frequency and time (m; rad/s; s). Dots mean time derivatives; every term in the mode equation has units of force. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. steps: Apply F(t) = (0.6,0.6) N cos(Ωt), where Ω is the drive angular frequency in rad/s.
The in-phase force is F₁(t) = (1.2/√2) N cos(Ωt) ≈ (0.848528 N) cos(Ωt).
The opposite-sign force is F₂(t) = (0.6 − 0.6)/√2 N cos(Ωt) = 0. From rest, mode 2 is not driven even if Ω equals its natural frequency.

lessons.title: Follow a moving shape, not a moving string piece
lessons.idea: A travelling wave moves a shape along the string; each small piece of string moves mainly up and down.
body: A travelling wave moves a shape along the string; each small piece of string moves mainly up and down.

Let f describe the shape at time zero. In f(x − vt), a feature keeps the same input value when x increases by vt. With v positive, the feature moves right. Replacing the minus with a plus makes it move left.

To find a string piece’s vertical velocity, hold its location x fixed and take the time derivative. The chain rule gives −v times the shape slope f′. A right-moving shape can therefore have a piece moving down at one point and up at another.
lessons.equation: y(x,t) = f(x − vt); u_y(x,t) = ∂y/∂t = −v f′(x − vt)
lessons.terms: x, y, t: along-string position, vertical displacement and time (m; m; s). x labels the approximate horizontal position of a material piece. v: positive propagation speed (m/s). This is not the vertical material velocity u_y. f, f′: shape function and its slope (m; dimensionless). The input is a distance in m. Prime means derivative with respect to that input. u_y, ∂: vertical material velocity and partial-derivative symbol (m/s; operator). Hold x fixed when differentiating in time. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. At a location where f′ = +0.02, the vertical velocity is −(3 m/s)(0.02) = −0.06 m/s.
The negative velocity means downward motion of that piece, not leftward travel of the crest.

lessons.title: Tension carries a bend along a string
lessons.idea: A curved string segment feels slightly different vertical pulls at its two ends.
body: A curved string segment feels slightly different vertical pulls at its two ends.

For a small slope, the vertical part of tension is approximately T times the slope ∂y/∂x. Subtract the left-end pull from the right-end pull. For a short length Δx the net vertical force is approximately T(∂²y/∂x²)Δx.

The segment has mass μΔx. Newton’s law equates its mass times vertical acceleration to that force. Cancel Δx to get the wave equation. Comparing it with a translating shape gives v² = T/μ; choose the positive square root for speed.
lessons.terms: T: constant string tension (N). T means force here, not period or temperature. μ: linear mass density (kg/m). Mass per unit length, positive and uniform. x, y, t, Δx: position, displacement, time and short segment length (m; m; s; m). ∂²y/∂t² is acceleration; ∂²y/∂x² is the small-slope curvature measure in m⁻¹. v: wave speed (m/s). The positive root of a positive tension-to-density ratio. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

steps: For T = 18 N and μ = 0.02 kg/m, T/μ = 900 m²/s².
The wave speed is √900 m/s = 30 m/s.
If the local curvature measure is +0.004 m⁻¹, the vertical acceleration is (900 m²/s²)(0.004 m⁻¹) = +3.6 m/s².

lessons.title: Count crests and the energy they carry
lessons.idea: A wavelength is the distance between repeating crests; a frequency counts how many cycles pass each second.
body: A wavelength is the distance between repeating crests; a frequency counts how many cycles pass each second.
One complete phase turn is 2π radians. Therefore k = 2π/λ counts phase change per metre and ω = 2πf counts phase change per second. The phase kx − ωt moves right at v = ω/k = fλ.

For one sinusoidal travelling wave on the ideal string, mean power is one half of μvω²A². A is the peak displacement, not a root-mean-square value. The factor one half comes from averaging the squared sine or cosine over a whole cycle. Doubling amplitude quadruples mean power.

lessons.terms: A, λ: peak displacement and wavelength (m). A is the largest displacement magnitude; λ is the repeat distance. k, ω, f: wave number, angular frequency and cycle frequency (rad/m; rad/s; Hz). k means wave number here, not spring stiffness. π is the circle constant. μ, v, P̄: linear density, wave speed and cycle-mean power (kg/m; m/s; W). The bar means an average over one cycle; power is energy transferred each second. x, t, y: position, time and displacement (m; s; m). The cosine argument is a phase in radians. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. lessons.title: A join can send part of a wave back
lessons.idea: At a joined string, the two ends must move together and their transverse forces must balance.
body: At a joined string, the two ends must move together and their transverse forces must balance.

Assume the same tension T on both sides and a massless join at x = 0. A wave arrives from side 1. Let r be reflected displacement amplitude divided by incident amplitude, including its sign; let tₐ be the transmitted ratio. Matching displacement gives 1 + r = tₐ.

The slopes of the reflected and incident waves have opposite propagation signs. Matching transverse tension gives Z₁(1 − r) = Z₂tₐ, where Z = T/v = √(Tμ) is the string’s mechanical impedance. Solving these two equations gives the ratios below.

A negative r flips the reflected displacement relative to the incident one. Energy fractions cannot be negative: reflection gives r², while transmission includes the impedance ratio. They add to 1 for this lossless join, even when tₐ exceeds 1.
lessons.equation: r = (Z₁ − Z₂)/(Z₁ + Z₂); tₐ = 2Z₁/(Z₁ + Z₂); R = r²; τ = (Z₂/Z₁)tₐ²; R + τ = 1
lessons.terms: Z₁, Z₂, T, μ, v: impedances, common tension, density and speed (kg/s; N; kg/m; m/s). Z measures transverse force relative to transverse velocity for a travelling wave; both impedances are positive. r, tₐ: signed displacement amplitude ratios (dimensionless). tₐ is a ratio, not time. Incident amplitude is nonzero. R, τ: reflected and transmitted mean-power fractions (dimensionless). Use power magnitudes in each propagation direction. τ is not a time constant. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

r = −1/3 and tₐ = 2/3. An incident 3 mm peak produces a reflected −1 mm signed amplitude and transmitted +2 mm amplitude.

lessons.title: Two travelling waves can make a stationary pattern
lessons.idea: A standing pattern keeps its quiet points in place even though the string between them moves.
body: A standing pattern keeps its quiet points in place even though the string between them moves.

Add two equal waves travelling in opposite directions: A sin(kx − ωt) and A sin(kx + ωt). The sine addition identity turns the sum into 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt). The first factor sets the position-dependent size; the cosine sets the time motion.

Nodes are points that stay at zero displacement at all times. They occur where sin(kx) = 0. Antinodes are halfway between neighbouring nodes and have the largest peak displacement, 2A. At an instant when the whole string passes through zero, those other points do not suddenly become nodes.

Each travelling component transports energy in its own direction. Their equal cycle-mean flows cancel. Energy can still move locally during a cycle; zero mean transport does not mean motion or energy is absent.
lessons.equation: y = 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt); x_node = nλ/2; x_antinode = (2n+1)λ/4
lessons.terms: A, λ: peak amplitude of each component and wavelength (m). The largest standing-wave peak is 2A, not A. k, ω: wave number and angular frequency (rad/m; rad/s). k = 2π/λ; both waves have the same positive values. x, t, n: position, time and integer location label (m; s; dimensionless). Choose integer n so the position lies on the considered string. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

Antinodes occur at x = 0.2, 0.6 m and so on, with peak displacement 0.003 m.
At x = 0.2 m and a time with cos(ωt) = −1, the displacement is −0.003 m.

lessons.title: The ends select which notes fit
lessons.idea: A string end can allow or forbid motion, and that selects its natural frequencies.
body: A string end can allow or forbid motion, and that selects its natural frequencies.

At a fixed end the transverse displacement is zero. With both ends fixed, the length L must contain a whole number n of half-wavelengths. The smallest frequency is the fundamental; the others are integer multiples called harmonics.

For a fixed end at x = 0 and an ideal freely sliding transverse end at x = L, the transverse force at the free end vanishes. With nonzero tension this means zero slope there. A node at one end and an antinode at the other fit an odd number of quarter-wavelengths. Only odd multiples of the fundamental occur in this ideal case.
lessons.equation: Fixed-fixed: fₙ = nv/(2L), n = 1,2,3,…; fixed-free: fₙ = (2n−1)v/(4L), n = 1,2,3,…
lessons.terms: fₙ: frequency of allowed mode n (Hz). n labels modes in order; for fixed-free, mode 2 is the third harmonic, not the second harmonic. v, L: wave speed and string length (m/s; m). Both are positive. The fundamental is the n=1 frequency. n, ∂y/∂x: positive integer mode label and slope (dimensionless). A free transverse end has slope zero; its displacement need not vanish. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

With the same length and speed but one fixed and one ideal free end, the first three frequencies are 8, 24 and 40 Hz.
The 24 Hz fixed-free mode is mode 2 and harmonic 3 because 24/8 = 3.

lessons.title: Assemble a string shape from allowed patterns
lessons.idea: A starting string shape can contain several allowed standing patterns at once.
body: A starting string shape can contain several allowed standing patterns at once.

For ends fixed at x = 0 and x = L, use sin(nπx/L). Each pattern is zero at both ends. Different integer patterns are orthogonal: the integral of their product over the string is zero; a pattern multiplied by itself integrates to L/2.

Multiply the starting shape g(x) by one pattern and integrate. The factor 2/L cancels that pattern’s L/2 factor, leaving its displacement coefficient aₙ. This projection isolates one pattern instead of guessing from the picture.

If the string starts at rest, each coefficient multiplies cos(ωₙt), where ωₙ = nπv/L. A nonzero starting velocity needs additional sine-in-time coefficients. The finite two-pattern example below is exact; an arbitrary shape generally needs a convergent series and may need many terms.
lessons.equation: aₙ = (2/L) ∫₀ᴸ g(x) sin(nπx/L) dx; y(x,t) = Σₙ aₙ sin(nπx/L) cos(ωₙt); ωₙ = nπv/L
lessons.terms: g, y, aₙ: starting shape, displacement and signed modal amplitude (m). g is y at t=0. The displayed time formula assumes zero initial velocity. x, L, dx: position, length and integration length element (m). ∫₀ᴸ adds contributions from x=0 to x=L. n, Σₙ, π: positive integer mode label, sum and circle constant (dimensionless). Sum all included modes. In the example only n=1 and n=2 are nonzero. v, ωₙ, t: wave speed, natural angular frequency and time (m/s; rad/s; s). Both sine and cosine arguments are dimensionless phases. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, J joule, W watt, Hz cycles per second; rad means radian. mm means millimetre, 0.001 m. A square or cube applies to the whole named unit.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Let L = 1 m and g(x) = (0.003 m) sin(πx/L) + (0.001 m) sin(2πx/L), with zero initial velocity.
For n = 1, the squared-sine integral is L/2 = 0.5 m and the mixed-sine integral is zero. Thus a₁ = (2/(1 m))[(0.003 m)(0.5 m)] = 0.003 m. Likewise a₂ = 0.001 m; all other coefficients are zero.
With v = 2 m/s, ω₁ = 2π rad/s and ω₂ = 4π rad/s. At x = L/2 and t = 0.25 s, the second spatial sine is zero and the first time cosine is zero, so y = 0 m.

lessons.title: Add waves before squaring
lessons.idea: A fixed phase decides whether two amplitudes reinforce or cancel.
body: Two waves can raise or lower the same displacement. Coherent means their relative timing, called phase, stays fixed during the observation. Write the signals as A₁ cos(ωt) and A₂ cos(ωt+δ). The amplitudes A₁ and A₂ are nonnegative; δ tells how far one cycle is shifted.

Adding the sine and cosine parts and squaring the resulting amplitude gives the relation below. The extra term is interference: it can be positive or negative. For the same medium and wave type, an intensity can be proportional to amplitude squared. Amplitude squared itself is not automatically a power.

If the relative phase wanders uniformly through a whole cycle, its cosine averages to zero. Then the averaged squared amplitude is A₁²+A₂², not (A₁+A₂)². That averaging assumption is what makes this an incoherent sum.
lessons.terms: A, A₁, A₂: resultant and individual displacement amplitudes (m). Nonnegative sizes. δ: relative phase (rad). Fixed for coherent addition. ω, t: angular frequency and time (rad/s; s). Both signals have the same ω; cos is cosine. Units: m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, Pa pascal (N/m²), J joule, W watt (J/s), V volt, mm millimetre (0.001 m), Hz hertz (cycles per second), and rad radian. A square means multiply by itself; / means per. π is about 3.14159; e is about 2.71828; √ takes the nonnegative square root. Trigonometric arguments are in radians. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units after converting prefixes.

lessons.title: Turn extra distance into phase
lessons.idea: Arrival phase depends on both the source timing and the extra path.
body: Choose the arrival signal on route j to be Aⱼ cos(ωt−kℓⱼ+φⱼ). Here ℓⱼ is its path length and φⱼ is its starting phase. An extra wavelength adds a full turn of phase. Both routes must be in the same uniform medium for one k to apply.

Subtract route 1’s phase from route 2’s phase. Define Δℓ=ℓ₂−ℓ₁ and Δφ=φ₂−φ₁. Then δ=Δφ−kΔℓ. Constructive addition has δ equal to an integer multiple of 2π. Opposite-phase addition has an odd multiple of π; cancellation is complete only if amplitudes also match.

lessons.idea: Two close frequencies produce repeated large and small oscillations.
body: Add two equal-amplitude oscillations with nearby positive frequencies f₁ and f₂. The cosine addition identity separates their sum into a fast carrier and a slowly changing multiplier, called an envelope. The carrier frequency is their average.

lessons.idea: A coefficient measures how much of a chosen sine or cosine is present.
body: A periodic signal repeats after a period T. Its Fourier series adds a constant, cosines and sines at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency Ω=2π/T. Use the convention q(t)=a₀/2+Σₙ₌₁∞[aₙ cos(nΩt)+bₙ sin(nΩt)]. The sum sign means add the terms for positive integers n.

To measure one cosine component, multiply the signal by that cosine and average over one period, then double the result. Different integer-frequency sines and cosines average to zero against one another. Matching squared sine or cosine averages to one half. The constant term a₀/2 is the ordinary average.
For q(t)=2 V+(3 V)cos(Ωt)−(1 V)sin(2Ωt), integration gives a₀=4 V, a₁=3 V and b₂=−1 V. For example a₁=(2/T)(3 V)(T/2)=3 V; all cross terms vanish. The other coefficients are zero.

lessons.title: Build a localized shape from many waves
lessons.idea: A finite-width shape needs a range of wave numbers, and its transform has different units.
body: A localized packet is large in a limited region rather than repeating forever at one wavelength. A Fourier integral adds a continuous range of wave numbers. Use the symmetric convention below; i is the imaginary unit with i²=−1, and exp(ikx) is shorthand for cos(kx)+i sin(kx). A real shape is recovered by combining paired positive and negative wave numbers.

Take a height h on −a<x<a and zero outside, where a>0. Integrating exp(−ikx) gives q̃(k)=2h sin(ka)/(√(2π)k) when k≠0. At k=0 use the limit sin(ka)/k→a, giving q̃(0)=2ah/√(2π). The spectrum is not confined to one k.

This transform describes the shape at a chosen time. Its later motion needs a dispersion relation, which tells the frequency belonging to each wave number. A sharp-edged box is a simple transform example, not a narrow-band smooth packet.

lessons.title: A narrower Gaussian needs a wider spectrum
lessons.idea: Shrinking a Gaussian in space or time broadens its spectrum.
body: Use the smooth, unchirped envelope q(x)=q₀ exp[−x²/(4σₓ²)]. Unchirped here means no extra position-dependent phase across that envelope; for the corresponding time pulse it means no extra time-dependent phase across its envelope. Define σₓ as the standard deviation of the normalized squared amplitude |q|², not of q itself. A standard deviation is a width obtained by averaging squared distance from the centre and taking the square root.

Its transform is proportional to exp(−σₓ²k²). Squaring that spectrum gives a Gaussian with standard deviation σₖ=1/(2σₓ). Thus these particular width definitions give σₓσₖ=1/2. A carrier shifts the spectrum’s centre but not these widths.

The same calculation for time gives σₜσω=1/2, where the widths come from squared signal and squared angular-frequency spectrum. Since ω=2πf, the ordinary-frequency width is σf=σω/(2π). These are classical shape relationships, not a claim about quantum measurement.

lessons.title: Sound moves compression along a fluid
lessons.idea: Compression and inertia together set sound speed, not the particle’s back-and-forth speed.
body: In a small longitudinal sound wave, fluid particles move back and forth along the travel direction. They do not travel along with the entire pattern. Let ξ(x,t) be their small displacement from equilibrium. A negative spatial slope ∂ξ/∂x crowds material together and raises the pressure.

The bulk modulus B measures resistance to compression: p′=−B∂ξ/∂x. Momentum balance gives ρ∂²ξ/∂t²=−∂p′/∂x. Substituting the pressure relation gives a wave equation with speed c=√(B/ρ). Here B is a compression modulus, not magnetic field.

For ξ=ξ₀cos(kx−ωt), pressure is p′=Bkξ₀sin(kx−ωt). Particle velocity is u=∂ξ/∂t=ωξ₀sin(kx−ωt). Pressure and particle velocity are in phase for this right-going wave; displacement is a quarter-cycle away. With ω=ck, their ratio is p′/u=ρc wherever u≠0.
lessons.terms: ξ, ξ₀, x: particle displacement, its peak and position (m). Small displacement gradient. p′, B: pressure change and bulk modulus (Pa). B>0; pressure change may be signed. ρ: equilibrium density (kg/m³). Positive and uniform. c, u: wave speed and signed particle velocity (m/s). Different physical quantities. t, k, ω: time, wave number and angular frequency (s; rad/m; rad/s). ∂ denotes a derivative holding the other variable fixed. Units: m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, Pa pascal (N/m²), J joule, W watt (J/s), V volt, mm millimetre (0.001 m), Hz hertz (cycles per second), and rad radian. A square means multiply by itself; / means per. π is about 3.14159; e is about 2.71828; √ takes the nonnegative square root. Trigonometric arguments are in radians. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units after converting prefixes.

lessons.title: Convert pressure into intensity and decibels
lessons.idea: Intensity depends on pressure squared; decibels describe a ratio, not a linear amount.
body: Intensity I is mean energy transfer per area per time. For one progressive plane sound wave in a lossless fluid, average p′u over a cycle. Since p′=ρcu and the average of sine squared is one half, a peak pressure p̂ gives I=p̂²/(2ρc).

Root-mean-square pressure p_rms means square, average, then square-root. For a sinusoid it is p̂/√2. The decibel intensity level L_I compares a positive intensity with a chosen reference I_ref using a base-ten logarithm. A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB; doubling pressure gives fourfold intensity, about 6.02 dB more.
lessons.terms: I, I_ref: mean intensity and reference intensity (W/m²). Here I_ref=10⁻¹² W/m². p̂, p_rms: peak and root-mean-square pressure (Pa). Nonnegative amplitude measures. ρ, c: density and sound speed (kg/m³; m/s). Their product is the progressive-wave pressure/velocity ratio. L_I, log₁₀: intensity level and base-ten logarithm (dB; none). log₁₀ asks what power of ten gives its dimensionless input. Units: m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton, Pa pascal (N/m²), J joule, W watt (J/s), V volt, mm millimetre (0.001 m), Hz hertz (cycles per second), and rad radian. lessons.title: A pipe end selects pressure patterns
lessons.idea: The end conditions decide which pressure and displacement patterns fit.
body: A rigid closed end prevents longitudinal particle motion: it is a displacement node, a point of zero oscillation, and a pressure antinode, a point of maximum pressure amplitude. An ideal open end holds the pressure change near zero: pressure node and displacement antinode.

Two ideal open ends therefore fit half-wavelengths into length L: λₙ=2L/n and fₙ=nc/(2L). One closed and one open end fit odd quarter-wavelengths: fₙ=(2n−1)c/(4L), with n=1,2,3,… counting allowed modes. The second allowed mode is the third harmonic, not twice the first frequency.

lessons.title: Count arriving crests in the medium frame
lessons.idea: A moving observer changes how quickly crests arrive; a moving source changes their spacing.
body: First keep the source and medium at rest. A source frequency f_s makes spacing λ=c/f_s between crests. An observer moving toward the source at speed u_o meets crests at relative speed c+u_o, so the observed rate is f_o=f_s(1+u_o/c). Toward is defined positive here; away can be represented by negative u_o.

Now use a different case: keep the observer at rest and move the source toward that observer at speed u_s. In one source period it advances u_s/f_s, making the forward spacing (c−u_s)/f_s. Hence f_o=f_s c/(c−u_s). The two formulas are not identical because sound has a medium frame.

lessons.title: A dispersion relation connects space and time
lessons.idea: A medium can assign different phase speeds to different wavelengths.
body: A sinusoidal component has phase kx−ωt. Its wave number k sets spatial repetition and its angular frequency ω sets temporal repetition. A dispersion relation ω(k) says which pairs the medium or model allows.

On a right-going branch k>0, the ideal nondispersive relation is ω=ck: every component has the same phase speed c. As a contrasting local model take ω=αk² with α>0. Here ω/k=αk, so shorter wavelengths on this branch have faster phase motion. α must have units m²/s for the formula to have angular-frequency units.

lessons.title: Follow a crest or follow a group
lessons.idea: The speed of a crest need not equal the speed of a narrow envelope.
body: To follow one constant phase, keep kx−ωt constant. Its speed is v_p=ω/k for k≠0. To follow the broad envelope of two close components, their phase difference Δk x−Δω t stays constant, giving envelope speed Δω/Δk.

As the components become close, that ratio becomes the derivative v_g=dω/dk. This group-speed approximation tracks a narrow packet only while higher-order changes do not strongly distort it. Neither formula alone proves the speed of the first new information in an arbitrary medium.

lessons.title: Dispersion can spread a packet
lessons.idea: Different component speeds can widen an initially smooth packet.
body: Nearby components have slightly different group speeds when the dispersion curve bends. Expand around centre k₀: ω≈ω₀+v_g(k−k₀)+(D/2)(k−k₀)². Here D=d²ω/dk² is the curvature, and ω₀=ω(k₀). The constant sets phase, the linear term translates the envelope, and the quadratic term changes its shape.

For an initially unchirped Gaussian, meaning no extra position-dependent phase across its envelope, the squared-amplitude width obeys the formula below under quadratic dispersion. The width σ₀ is the initial standard deviation defined earlier, not the full visible width. Negative curvature spreads this particular initial Gaussian as well, because D is squared.

For ω=αk² the expansion is exact and D=2α. For another smooth relation it is only a local approximation over the occupied wave-number range. Neglecting curvature predicts translation without spreading and can fail at long times.

lessons.title: Below cutoff, a component decays in space
lessons.idea: A cutoff can replace spatial oscillation with exponential decay.
body: Consider the stated one-dimensional relation ω²=ω_c²+c₀²k², with positive cutoff ω_c and speed parameter c₀. For ω>ω_c, k is real and a sinusoidal spatial pattern can propagate. For 0<ω<ω_c, k² is negative, so write k=iκ with κ>0 for the solution that decays toward +x.

The factor exp(ikx) then becomes exp(−κx). This is called evanescent: it oscillates in time but decreases with distance instead of having a real spatial wavelength. The length 1/κ is the distance over which its amplitude falls by a factor e. The squared amplitude is divided by e² over that same distance.

At exact cutoff k=0, division by k cannot define a finite phase speed. For a finite region, both increasing and decreasing exponential terms may be needed to match its two boundaries. Evanescence does not by itself imply exactly zero transmission through every finite barrier.

lessons.title: Keep field direction separate from travel direction
lessons.idea: In a vacuum plane wave, the electric and magnetic fields point across the direction of travel.
body: Choose a wave travelling along positive x. Let its electric component point along y and its magnetic component along z: E_y=E₀cos(kx−ωt) and B_z=(E₀/c)cos(kx−ωt). Both components share the same phase, so their zeros and signed peaks occur together.

The field vectors are perpendicular to each other and to the travel direction. Their directions can reverse together while the energy still flows forward. The Poynting vector S=(E×B)/μ₀ describes electromagnetic energy flow per area; y crossed with z points along positive x, and reversing both factors keeps that direction.

For a sinusoidal vacuum wave, mean intensity is I=½ε₀cE₀². E₀ is a peak, not an average. The one-half comes from averaging cosine squared. A field oscillation is not a material object riding along at light speed, and the wave speed is not a charge’s drift speed.
lessons.terms: E_y, E₀, B_z: Signed electric component, peak electric size and signed magnetic component (V/m, V/m, T). Subscripts y and z name spatial directions; zero labels peak amplitude here. k, x, ω, t, c: Wave number, position, angular frequency, time and vacuum wave speed (rad/m, m, rad/s, s, m/s). k=ω/c>0; use rounded c≈3.0×10⁸ m/s for the example. S, I: Instantaneous energy-flow vector and mean intensity (W/m²). Mean is over a full sinusoidal cycle; intensity is nonnegative in the travel direction. μ₀, ε₀: Vacuum permeability and permittivity (H/m, F/m). Use ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ε₀=1/c² in vacuum. × is the vector cross product. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A slash means per; squared means multiplied by itself. Quantity names such as k or T are defined for this lesson. Bare-number arithmetic uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining scales. nm means nanometre (10⁻⁹ m); mm means millimetre (10⁻³ m); cm means centimetre (10⁻² m). In optics V means volt, T tesla, and W/m² is power per area. Input tolerances permit rounding, not measurement or safety claims. H means henry, the inductance unit; F means farad, the capacitance unit. Thus H/m and F/m mean those units per metre.

apply.text: Would choosing E₀ and B₀ independently still describe this vacuum plane wave?
apply.answer: Not generally. Maxwell’s equations require B₀=E₀/c for the stated travelling wave. A different ratio may describe some other field arrangement, but cannot be silently inserted into this plane-wave model.

lessons.title: Describe how the electric direction changes
lessons.idea: Polarization describes the path of the electric-field tip at one fixed place.
body: Now choose propagation along positive z, so the transverse plane is x-y. Write E_x=A_x cosψ and E_y=A_y cos(ψ+δ), where ψ=ωt−kz. Here A_x and A_y are nonnegative component peaks, and δ is their relative phase. Changing axes is deliberate: travel is now along z, not x.

When δ=0 or π, the components stay in a fixed signed ratio and the field tip follows a line: linear polarization. For equal nonzero component peaks and δ=±π/2, the field tip follows a circle with constant magnitude. Other generic amplitude/phase combinations make an ellipse; a zero component gives a line.

This curve is traced by the field vector at one place, not a particle flying around a circle. For an explicit rotation convention, draw x right and y up and look against the +z travel direction. With δ=−π/2 and equal peaks, increasing time takes the vector from +x toward +y, counterclockwise in this drawing. Avoid an unqualified “right-handed” label: naming conventions depend on viewing direction.

Component peaks are not always the maximum size of the combined field. ψ, δ: Shared phase and y-relative-to-x phase (rad). The sign of δ follows the displayed cosine convention. ω, k, t, z: Angular frequency, wave number, time and travel coordinate (rad/s, rad/m, s, m). Fix z while watching the vector change with time; ω and k are positive for this +z wave.
