Correct. The electric field remains on the x direction, reversing its sign each half cycle.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can a circle in this diagram prove that light particles travel along corkscrews?
apply.answer: No. The plotted tip represents the local electric vector as time changes. It is not the position of a particle and does not give a particle trajectory. The wave’s propagation direction and the field’s transverse time dependence are different pieces of the model.

lessons.limits: Monochromatic coherent transverse components in a fixed Cartesian frame. A zero field has no defined polarization direction; partially polarized statistical mixtures need additional information.

lessons.title: A polarizer keeps one field component
lessons.idea: An ideal linear polarizer transmits the electric component along its allowed axis.
body: For linearly polarized incident light, let θ be the angle between its electric direction and the polarizer’s transmission axis. The transmitted field amplitude is E_out=E_in cosθ. Squaring the amplitude gives Malus’s law I_out=I_in cos²θ for ideal transmission in the same medium.

If the incident light is unpolarized, there is no single fixed incident direction. Average over equally represented transverse directions: the average of cos²θ is one half. An ideal first polarizer then transmits I_in/2 and makes the output linearly polarized along its own axis.

For several polarizers, use the angle between each new axis and the polarization coming from the previous one. Multiplying each stage’s intensity fraction is not the same as applying just the total first-to-last angle. Real polarizers also absorb and scatter beyond this ideal projection model.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why must the word “unpolarized” not be treated as a 90-degree angle?
apply.answer: Unpolarized light is a statistical mixture rather than one fixed electric direction. The first polarizer averages over directions; it is not perpendicular to all of them. The half-intensity result differs from the zero transmission of a linearly polarized beam crossed by 90°.

lessons.title: Match the phase along an interface
lessons.idea: A wave crossing a flat boundary must keep the same timing and along-boundary phase.
body: Let a monochromatic wave reach a stationary plane boundary between two transparent uniform media. Angle θ is measured from the normal, the direction perpendicular to the surface. A crest must meet the boundary with compatible phase on both sides, so the frequency stays the same and the tangential wave-number component matches.

That matching gives k₁sinθ₁=k₂sinθ₂. With refractive index n=c/v_p and k=nω/c, this becomes n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂. This is Snell’s law. Here v_p is phase speed, and the indices are evaluated at the wave’s frequency. It is not a rule that frequency changes when light enters a medium.

If n₁>n₂, increasing θ₁ eventually makes the required sinθ₂ exceed 1. The critical angle satisfies sinθ_c=n₂/n₁. Above it there is no propagating transmitted ray in this ideal lossless two-half-space geometry. A decaying field can still exist across the boundary; “total internal reflection” does not mean the field is identically zero there.

Indices 1 and 2 label incident and transmitted media. n₁, n₂, n: Refractive indices (no unit). n=c/v_p; assume positive real indices and lossless isotropic media at this frequency. θ₁, θ₂, θ_c: Incidence, transmission and critical angles (degrees in examples; radians also valid). All angles are measured from the normal, not the surface. ω, c, v_p: Shared angular frequency, vacuum speed and phase speed (rad/s, m/s, m/s). Frequency is unchanged at a stationary interface; wavelength can change. apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does Snell’s law alone tell us what fraction of power is reflected?
apply.answer: No. It determines allowed phase directions, not reflection and transmission amplitudes. Those require matching the electromagnetic boundary conditions and depend on polarization. Fuller Fresnel coefficients and thin-film effects belong to the separate Optics path.

lessons.limits: Stationary planar interface, monochromatic waves, transparent isotropic media with positive real refractive indices. Finite gaps, absorption, anisotropy and evanescent coupling require additional analysis.

lessons.title: Turn a path difference into bright and dark directions
lessons.idea: Two coherent paths can reinforce or cancel at a screen.
body: Consider two narrow equal slits separated by centre-to-centre distance d, illuminated in phase at wavelength λ in the surrounding medium. Far from the slits, the path difference is Δℓ=d sinθ, where θ is measured from the forward normal.

The phase difference is δ=2πΔℓ/λ. If each slit alone gives intensity I₁ at that angle and the polarizations match, adding equal field amplitudes gives I=4I₁cos²(δ/2). Maximum intensity is four times one-slit intensity because amplitudes add before squaring; it is not four times the total incident energy.

Bright directions obey d sinθ=mλ, with integer order m. For a distant flat screen and small angles, y≈Lθ and sinθ≈θ, giving fringe spacing Δy≈λL/d. Here L is screen distance and y is transverse screen position. Large angles require the exact sine geometry and y=Ltanθ instead.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If the two sources fluctuate independently in phase, should perfect dark fringes remain?
apply.answer: Not in the time-averaged pattern described here. Stable cancellation needs a stable relative phase. For uncorrelated phase fluctuations, the interference cross term averages away and mean intensities add; the coherent equal-phase formula is then not applicable.

lessons.title: Add contributions across one opening
lessons.idea: Even one slit can send different parts of its field out with different phases.
body: Let a uniformly illuminated slit have width a along coordinate ξ, from −a/2 to +a/2. In the far field at angle θ, a point at ξ contributes phase kξsinθ relative to the slit centre. Add these complex amplitudes across the opening: the normalized amplitude is (1/a)∫ exp(i kξsinθ)dξ over the slit.

Integrating gives sinβ/β, where β=πa sinθ/λ and k=2π/λ. Here i²=−1; the complex calculation keeps phases, and the real physical field comes from the oscillating real part. The imaginary contributions cancel for a symmetric uniformly lit slit. The function sincβ here specifically means sinβ/β, not the alternate convention sin(πβ)/(πβ).

Intensity is I=I₀(sinβ/β)², where I₀ is the on-axis intensity for this same setup. At β=0 use the limit sinβ/β→1, not division by zero. The first minima occur at a sinθ=±λ. Far-field conditions and uniform illumination are essential; an arbitrary nearby screen need not show this exact pattern.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does I₀ stay the same automatically if slit width changes?
apply.answer: No. I₀ is the on-axis intensity for the stated aperture and illumination. Changing the aperture can change transmitted power and the on-axis value. The normalized formula describes shape; it does not say that every changed physical slit has the same absolute peak intensity.

lessons.title: Many openings sharpen the principal directions
lessons.idea: A finite row of coherent slits produces narrow principal peaks with a finite width.
body: For N identical narrow equally spaced slits, the phase step between neighbours is δ=2πd sinθ/λ. Adding the geometric series of field amplitudes gives a normalized array intensity factor [sin(Nδ/2)/(N sin(δ/2))]². At a principal peak both numerator and denominator vanish; take the limit, which is 1 in this normalized convention.

Principal directions obey d sinθ=mλ. This condition locates peaks but does not say how narrow they are. Finite N leaves a finite angular width, roughly set by the neighbouring zeros of the numerator. Increasing illuminated slit count sharpens the array peaks under the same ideal assumptions.

The Rayleigh-style criterion calls two comparable spectral peaks just resolved when the centre of one falls at the first minimum beside the other. For an ideal grating with many illuminated slits, a sharp accessible non-grazing order |m|>0, small wavelength separation and this criterion, resolving power is R=λ/Δλ≈|m|N. Here Δλ is the smallest wavelength separation predicted by that criterion near λ. Real slit width, unequal illumination, aberrations and detector sampling can limit performance further. The zeroth order is not a useful wavelength-dispersing order. The array-factor formula still makes sense for N=1, but a single slit has no separate grating-array orders or neighbouring array minima; the grating resolving-power estimate does not apply to that case.
lessons.equation: δ=2πd sinθ/λ;  A_N=[sin(Nδ/2)/(N sin(δ/2))]²;  d sinθ=mλ;  R=λ/Δλ≈|m|N

A_N: Normalized array intensity factor (no unit). Despite its letter A, this is the explicitly defined squared intensity ratio, not an electric amplitude. m, λ, θ: Integer order, wavelength and observation angle (no unit, m, rad or degrees as stated). Allowed orders require |mλ/d|≤1. R, Δλ: Resolving power and wavelength separation (no unit, m). R is not circuit resistance here; the estimate assumes nonzero order and ideal criterion-limited optics. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Let d=2.0 μm and λ=500 nm. For order m=2, sinθ=2λ/d=0.5, so θ=30°.
With N=200 illuminated slits, the ideal resolving power in that order is about R=400.

The corresponding separation estimate is Δλ≈(500 nm)/400=1.25 nm. This is an ideal wavelength-discrimination estimate, not the angular separation between the grating orders. Here μm means micrometre, 10⁻⁶ m.

To evaluate the array factor itself, separately take N=4 and adjacent phase δ=π/2. Then sin(Nδ/2)=sinπ=0, while Nsin(δ/2)=4sin(π/4) is nonzero. The normalized array intensity is therefore zero: this direction is dark in the ideal four-slit array.

check.prompt: At fixed nonzero order, the illuminated slit count doubles. What happens to the ideal Δλ estimate?
explanations: Correct. R≈|m|N doubles, so Δλ≈λ/R halves.
More equal coherent slits sharpen the ideal peak, not broaden it.
The slit count appears in the ideal resolution estimate.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does a missing high order mean the resolving-power formula is wrong?
apply.answer: Not necessarily. The order must first satisfy |mλ/d|≤1, and a finite slit envelope can suppress a direction. Resolution is meaningful only for an accessible observed order and the stated illumination; the compact formula is not a guarantee that every integer order exists.

lessons.limits: Finite coherent array with identical narrow slits and equal illumination; nonzero accessible order. Ideal Rayleigh-style resolution only, not a complete instrument specification. The resolving-power estimate assumes many illuminated slits, small wavelength separation and a sharp accessible non-grazing order; it is not a one-slit resolution rule.

lessons.title: Choose the model before the formula
lessons.idea: The same word “wave” does not give every system the same physical assumptions.
body: A discrete mass-and-spring model follows a few coordinates. An ideal string wave follows a displacement field y(x,t) under tension. Sound follows small pressure and density changes in a medium. An electromagnetic wave follows electric and magnetic fields. These quantities have different units even when their equations share a similar shape.

For example, string speed is v=√(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per length. Sound speed in the stated bulk model is c_s=√(B/ρ), where B is bulk modulus and ρ mass per volume. Vacuum light speed is c. Do not transplant a string tension into an acoustic or electromagnetic formula just because all three outputs are speeds.

List the initial data, forcing, boundary conditions and approximation limits before calculating. A selected mode frequency is not automatically the frequency of an external source. A group velocity is not automatically a universal information-speed limit. An angle diagram is not automatically a particle trajectory.
lessons.equation: Ideal string: v=√(T/μ);  bulk acoustic model: c_s=√(B/ρ);  vacuum EM: c≈3.0×10⁸ m/s
lessons.terms: v, c_s, c: String wave, sound and vacuum light speeds (m/s). These symbols describe different models, not interchangeable material constants. T, μ: String tension and mass per length (N, kg/m). T is tension here, not period or tesla; μ is not magnetic permeability. B, ρ: Bulk modulus and mass density (Pa=N/m², kg/m³). B is material resistance to compression here, not magnetic field. The acoustic medium must match the assumed modulus. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). Correct. T and μ are the inputs to v=√(T/μ).
Vacuum light speed does not depend on the string tension.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What should you do if a question asks for a standing-wave frequency but omits the boundary conditions?
apply.answer: Do not guess fixed ends. Boundary conditions select the permitted mode pattern and wavelength. Ask for or explicitly state the end constraints, then calculate. A plausible number without a justified physical model is not a complete solution.

lessons.limits: Model-selection practice for already introduced introductory systems. It does not certify independent design skill, safety or mastery of all wave phenomena.

lessons.title: Connect a string mode to its driven response
lessons.idea: A natural pattern and a driven response can be analysed in steps without treating them as the same thing.
body: Take an ideal uniform string of length L fixed at both ends. Small transverse waves travel at v=√(T/μ). The fundamental standing mode has wavelength 2L, frequency f₁=v/(2L), and angular frequency ω₁=2πf₁.

Write the mode displacement as y(x,t)=q(t)sin(πx/L). The coordinate q is the displacement at the middle, where sine is one. For this specific normalization, the mode mass is M=μL/2. A point force at the centre projects onto this mode with the same signed force value; other force positions or shapes need their own projection.

In a stated single-mode approximation with linear damping b, the mode equation is Mq̈+bq̇+Mω₁²q=F₀cos(ωt). At drive ω=ω₁, the steady centre amplitude is A=F₀/(bω₁). This is a projection model near the fundamental, not a claim that the exact string has only one mode. Other modes and transient motion can matter. Here t is elapsed time in seconds, q̇ is dq/dt in m/s and q̈ is d²q/dt² in m/s². The choice ω=ω₁ tunes to the undamped natural frequency and, for fixed force amplitude in this damped single-mode model, the absorbed-power peak. It is not the exact displacement-amplitude maximum when damping is finite.
lessons.equation: v=√(T/μ);  f₁=v/(2L);  M=μL/2;  A=F₀/(bω₁) at ω=ω₁
lessons.terms: T, μ, L, v: Tension, linear density, length and wave speed (N, kg/m, m, m/s). Uniform taut string with fixed ends and small slopes. f₁, ω₁, ω: Fundamental frequency, its angular frequency and drive angular frequency (Hz, rad/s, rad/s). ω₁=2πf₁. The source selects ω; natural-frequency tuning is the special choice ω=ω₁; this is the fixed-force power peak, not generally the damped displacement peak. q, y, x, M: Mode coordinate, local displacement, along-string coordinate and mode mass (m, m, m, kg). The sinusoidal mode shape is normalized to one at the centre; M=μL/2 applies to that normalization. F₀, b, A: Peak projected force, mode damping and centre amplitude (N, kg/s, m). F₀≥0, b>0; single-mode late-time approximation. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). steps: Let T=40 N, μ=0.010 kg/m and L=1.0 m. Then v≈63.25 m/s, f₁≈31.62 Hz, ω₁≈198.69 rad/s and mode mass M=0.0050 kg.
At the centre, apply peak force F₀=0.010 N and choose mode damping b=0.020 kg/s. Drive at ω₁. The steady amplitude is A≈0.010/(0.020×198.69) m≈0.00252 m.
The mean damping loss is ½bω₁²A²=F₀²/(2b)=0.0025 W. This balance checks the response calculation, but it does not remove the small-slope and single-mode assumptions.

check.prompt: Double the tension with μ and L unchanged. How does the fundamental natural frequency change?
explanations: The speed and frequency depend on the square root of tension.
Changing tension changes the restoring force and wave speed.
Correct. f₁=√(T/μ)/(2L), so the natural frequency scales by √2.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If the source frequency is not retuned after changing tension, is the drive still tuned to the natural frequency?
apply.answer: Not generally. The source keeps its chosen frequency while the string’s natural frequency changes. The natural-frequency shortcut A=F₀/(bω₁) then no longer applies. Use the off-resonant amplitude with the new natural frequency and the actual source frequency.

lessons.title: Keep projection, interference and diffraction separate
lessons.idea: A combined optical calculation works only when each stage’s assumptions stay visible.
body: Start with a linearly polarized beam and an ideal polarizer at relative angle θ_p. Its intensity fraction is cos²θ_p. Next consider a uniformly illuminated slit: its normalized diffraction shape is [sinβ/β]², where β=πa sinθ/λ.

If the polarizer scales the illumination uniformly without changing wavelength or aperture shape, it scales the intensity at every observation angle by its transmission fraction. Define I₀ here as the slit’s on-axis intensity without that polarizer, not the intensity incident on the aperture. Then I(θ)=I₀cos²θ_p[sinβ/β]² under the stated model.

For a double-slit version, an additional coherent phase factor is needed; do not insert it into a single-slit calculation. State whether the screen geometry uses exact sine/tangent angles or a small-angle approximation. A correct final number without these conditions does not demonstrate justified model selection.
lessons.terms: I(θ), I₀: Observed intensity and no-polarizer on-axis reference intensity (W/m²). I₀ refers to this same slit and incident beam before inserting the uniform ideal polarizer. θ_p, θ: Polarizer relative angle and observation angle (degrees or radians as specified). They are different angles in different physical roles. a, λ, β: Slit width, wavelength and diffraction argument (m, m, rad). At β=0 use sinc limit one. One single slit is assumed, not a slit pair. Unit labels: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). example.title: Try one concrete case
steps: Let the reference I₀=100 W/m² and polarizer angle θ_p=60°. On axis, the transmitted intensity is 100cos²60°=25 W/m².
At an observation angle with β=π/2, multiply by 4/π². The intensity is 25×4/π²≈10.13 W/m².
At the first slit minimum β=π, the ideal intensity is zero regardless of this finite polarizer transmission. A polarizer does not shift the minimum in this uniform-scaling model.

explanations: Correct. The polarizer rescales illumination uniformly here; a sinθ=λ still sets the first minimum.
The slit width and wavelength, not the polarizer angle, set this minimum.
The on-axis point remains a maximum if transmission is nonzero.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Which assumption would fail if the filter blocked one side of the slit more than the other?
apply.answer: Uniform illumination scaling would fail. The amplitude sum across the slit would have a new weighting, so the original sinc pattern need not retain the same shape or exact dark minima. Recompute the aperture amplitude rather than multiplying the old pattern by one constant.
